blocks.text: Gas chromatography (GC) separates gases, volatile liquids and solids in the gaseous form. The stationary phase is a non-volatile, high-boiling liquid, such as a long-chain non-polar hydrocarbon, bonded to small particles of silica (SiO2) or alumina (Al2O3). The mobile phase is an inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen. The sample is injected into an injector port, where an oven vaporises it quickly, and the carrier gas takes the vapour through a long coiled column packed with tiny particles with a large surface area, where the separation happens.

Non-polar substances in the mixture interact more strongly with the non-polar liquid on the particles of the stationary phase, so they are carried through the column more slowly. Substances that interact strongly move slowly while others move faster, and so they separate. As the separated substances leave the column they pass through a detector, which records them as peaks on a graph called a chromatogram. The time a substance takes to pass through the column is its retention time.

blocks.alt: Top: carrier gas (helium or nitrogen) enters an injector port where the sample is injected and vaporised; the gas carries it through a coiled column in an oven to a detector and out, and a recorder draws the chromatogram. Bottom: a chromatogram of detector signal against retention time with three triangular peaks A, B and C, and the formulas area of a peak = 1/2 x base x height and % of A = area of A / sum of areas x 100.
blocks.caption: The gas chromatograph and a chromatogram (original diagram after Figure 28.5).
blocks.long_description: Each component leaves the column at its own retention time, which identifies it. The area under each peak is proportional to the amount of that component, so comparing areas gives the composition of the mixture.

blocks.text: GC has high sensitivity, good resolution, fast analysis and accurate quantification; mixtures of gases are easily separated at room temperature. It is a quantitative technique: the peaks are identified and the area of each is measured to give the proportion of each component. Because the peaks are roughly triangular, area of a peak = 1/2 x base x height, and, for a mixture of three esters A, B and C, % of A = (peak area of A / sum of peak areas of A, B and C) x 100. If the peaks are very narrow or have similar base widths, peak height is used instead of area. GC is used to check for steroids in athletes and to test fuels used in car racing.

items: Industry: quality control and environmental protection; petrochemical plants analyse fuels, and trace organic pollutants are detected in environmental samples.
Forensic science: blood alcohol content (BAC) tests and the detection of illegal drugs, poisons and performance-enhancing substances in biological samples.
Food and drink: checking consistency and safety, detecting spoilage by bacteria or fungi before it is visible, and analysing perfumes, essential oils and flavourings.
Medicine: diagnosing metabolic disorders from compounds in breath or urine, and checking new drugs for residual solvents or impurities.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: A man in China accused in 2005 of poisoning two neighbouring children with rat poison (a fluoroacetate) was released in 2013, eight years later, after gas chromatography showed that the food sample contained no poison.

items: It works only for volatile (easily vaporised) substances.
Samples must be thermally stable; compounds that decompose at high temperature cannot be analysed.
Large biomolecules such as proteins and polymers cannot be analysed because they do not vaporise easily.
The instruments and their maintenance are expensive.
